title: How to strip floss for cross-stitch
subtitle: Separating the strands before threading for smooth, even coverage
excerpt: Stripping floss means taking a cut length and pulling the strands apart individually before re-combining them for threading. It removes the twist that built up in manufacture and lets the strands lie flat and parallel in the finished stitch, giving coverage that looks even on the fabric.
sourceNotes: Standard cross-stitch preparation technique. Documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive, and all major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count and threads them together.

content.text: means pulling each strand away individually before combining the number you need. Cross-stitch thread has six strands twisted together. When you use two strands without stripping, they carry the twist of manufacture into the stitch, which makes the coverage look thin and uneven. Strip first and the strands lie parallel and flat.

Cut a length of no more than 40 cm (about 16 inches) before you strip. Longer lengths tangle more easily and are harder to control. The cut length is stripped all at once, then the separated strands are re-combined before threading the needle.
Cut a length of floss (maximum 40 cm) from the skein. Hold the cut length between the thumb and forefinger of one hand, close to the top. Let the rest of the length hang free.

Use the other hand to grasp a single strand at the very top of the cut length. Pull it straight upward, away from the rest. The other strands will bunch and ruffle as the one strand slides out. Let them gather and keep pulling.

The strand should come free in a single smooth pull. If it tangles, relax the other strands by letting them drop and shaking gently. A strand that won't pull free usually means the length is too long or the floss has been kinked.

Repeat for each strand you need. For 14-count Aida use two strands; strip and set them aside individually, then lay them together before threading. The strands should lie parallel and smooth when placed alongside each other.
Thread both stripped strands together through the needle eye. The needle carries them in parallel, not twisted. The resulting thread should feel soft and flat in your fingers.

items.symptom: Strands tangle and knot as you pull them out
items.cause: The cut length is too long, or you are pulling too fast.
items.fix: Work with lengths no longer than 40 cm. Pull the single strand slowly and steadily. If the other strands bunch too much, pause and let them drop and settle before continuing the pull.

items.symptom: Stitches still look thin even after stripping
items.cause: The strands were re-twisted when threading rather than kept parallel.
items.fix: After stripping, hold the two strands side by side with no twist between them as you thread the needle. Feed them into the eye together but don't loop them; they should sit flat and parallel through the eye.

content.text: Strip a few test lengths and stitch a small row of crosses without stripping, then a row with stripped strands. The difference in coverage is clear even on a scrap of Aida. After that, the habit forms quickly.
